title: Microstructural design strategy to maintain the brittle fracture toughness of hard-soft dual phase steel after cyclic plastic strain
abstract: Superstructures are seriously damaged because of plastic deformation when natural disasters, such as large earthquakes or unexpectedly large waves, occur. Therefore, there is a need to develop materials that are resistant to damage and fracture while maintaining a certain level of strength. In this paper, the difference in material toughness changes when cyclic prestrain occurs among different ferrite/pearlite two-phase microstructures were investigated. Synthetic analysis using strain gradient plasticity (SGP) theory, one of the crystal plasticity theories, was carried out, and conventional macroscopic material damage consideration rules were employed. Then, it was suggested that the amount of material damage changes among the different microstructures. In addition, a parametric study using SGP theory is performed to suggest directions for the microstructural design of steel with a lower risk of brittle fracture due to plastic deformation. As a result, damage-resistant materials with sufficient strength can be proposed.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Steel materials are used for many applications, such as high-rise buildings, large structures, large ships and infrastructure and pipe lines and tanks for transporting and storing liquefied natural gas, due to their superior strength and low cost. These structures have become increasingly larger due to increased demand, and the risk of brittle fracture steadily increases. In addition, these structures are seriously damaged because of plastic deformation when natural disasters, such as large earthquakes or unexpectedly large waves, occur, which also increases the risk of brittle fracture. For steel materials, brittle fracture is an unavoidable problem that should be considered as intrinsically possible, so there is a need to develop materials that are resistant to damage and fracture while maintaining a certain level of strength. In this context, it is important to understand the micromechanism of brittle fracture and the effect of plastic strain on the toughness of steel materials.

First, historical aspect of the research on the micromechanism of brittle fracture in steel are presented. Brittle fracture is considered to originate from microcracks in materials, and the most famous equation that describes the combinations of microcracks and brittle fracture is the classical Griffith eq. [ 1 ]. This equation is based on Inglis's eq. [ 2 ] and the second law of thermodynamics and explains that cracks start to propagate and fracture occurs if the stress exceeds critical stress. However, the critical stress obtained from the experiment is much lower than the theoretical fracture strength predicted by Griffith's equation. Therefore, it was considered that different mechanisms influenced the fracture in steel. Stroh [ 3 ] suggested that dislocation pile-up from plastic deformation affected the fracture behavior. This is based on the Hall-Petch equation [ 4 , 5 ], which shows that the yield stress depends on the grain size and that brittle fracture is dominated by the formulation of microcracks. Later, Cottrell [ 6 ] suggested that brittle fracture is dominated not only by the formation but also by the growth of microcracks. Based on Cottrell's theory, Smith [ 7 ] and Petch [ 8 ] suggested that the critical stress is determined by the grain size and the thickness of the carbide particle at the grain boundary. Generally, dislocations are piled-up to form carbide particles at grain boundaries due to the plastic deformation when tensile stress is loaded. Piled-up dislocations cause stress concentrations, which generate microcracks at carbide particles. In addition, the mechanism of brittle fracture for various microstructures was developed [ 9–11 ]. Also, fracture prediction mode has been improved by using the finite element method (FEM) [ 12 ].

Based on Smith's eq. [ 7 ], loading plastic deformation is equivalent to an increase in piled-up dislocations, which increases the risk of brittle fracture. It was experimentally confirmed that the formation of microcracks is greatly promoted by loading plastic deformation [ 13 , 14 ]. Thus, material damage progresses due to loading plastic deformation when natural disasters, such as earthquakes or large ocean waves, occur, which is evident due to the deterioration of the fracture toughness, including the Charpy impact characteristic after prestrain in the experimental room.

There has been previous work on the effect of prestrain on the fracture toughness. An et al. [ 15 ] showed that the ductile-brittle transition temperature of the Charpy impact test rose when tensile prestrain was loaded. Miki et al. [ 16 ] showed that the transition temperature of the crack tip opening displacement (CTOD) test rose when tensile and compressive prestrain was loaded, and the amount of deterioration was larger in compressive prestrain than in tensile prestrain. However, Fukuda et al. [ 17 ] showed that both the tensile and compressive prestrain values of approximately 5% deteriorated the toughness, but there was no significant difference between them. Kosuge et al. [ 18 ] showed that critical quasi-CTOD decreased when prestrain was loaded in various directions. In addition, Madi et al. [ 19 ] showed that the amount of deterioration depended on the strain hardening of the material.

In summary, it has been experimentally confirmed that a single prestrain scenario deteriorates the fracture toughness, but there have been few experimental results about the deterioration after complicated prestrain, such as cyclic prestrain assuming earthquakes. In the engineering field, the Coffin-Manson equation [ 20 , 21 ] has mainly been used as an estimation measure for material damage. This is a life prediction formula for low cycle fatigue, and the equivalent plastic strain is simply considered to be the material damage. However, Okura et al. [ 22 ] showed that deterioration after cyclic prestrain can be evaluated using skeletal plastic strain instead of equivalent plastic strain. In addition, Ohata et al. [ 23 ] and Kawabata et al. [ 24 ] suggested that material damage progresses only when the maximum value of equivalent back stress is updated during cyclic plastic strain. Additionally, Kosuge et al. [ 25 ] showed that not only the amount but also the order of prestrain had a great impact on the deterioration after cyclic prestrain. In this way, although it has been variably confirmed that fracture toughness deteriorates when plastic prestrain is loaded, a material damage estimation rule that is truly useful in the engineering field should be investigated in more detail.

Additionally, considering that steel material is intrinsically inhomogeneous microscopically and has various complex microstructures that have different physical properties, the effect of a mixture of microstructures on the material damage due to cyclic prestrain should be clarified. There are many studies on the deformation law and stress-strain curve for multiphase structural materials [ 26–30 ]. However, there is little research regarding fracture toughness. Shoji et al. [ 31 ] showed that ductile fracture resistance can be enhanced by changing the morphology of ferrite and pearlite geometrical allocation into layered types from random types. However, this approach remains an interpretation of actual experiments, and the detailed mechanism and universal knowledge have not been shown. Furthermore, to the authors' best knowledge, there is no publication regarding material damage toward brittle fracture. In this paper, using several cyclic prestraining patterns on three steel materials that have different kinds of microstructures, brittle fracture toughness deteriorations are observed. Based on the results, the material damage estimation rule for brittle fracture toughness is discussed by using the FEM, incorporating both a continuum mechanics model and a crystal plasticity model. Finally, a parametric study using the FEM is performed to suggest directions for the microstructural design of steel with less increased risk of brittle fracture due to earthquakes and unexpectedly large ocean waves.

sections.heading: Experiment
paragraphs: In this section, the methods for the prestrain test and fracture test and their results are explained. Several cyclic prestrains were loaded onto three types of steel plates with different microstructures, followed by Charpy impact tests as a measure of the brittle fracture toughness.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs:
To vary the fraction of the hard phase and soft phase, a simple ferrite and pearlite combination microstructure that is widely used for structural steels was chosen. To step through the ratio of ferrite and pearlite, the content of carbon was changed when the rest of the chemical composition was constant, as shown in  Table 1 
                         . Here, impurities (P, S, N, and O), which cause microscopic strain concentrations, were suppressed as much as possible. Ingots were prepared with a thickness of 100 mm after adjusting the chemical composition using a 180-kg vacuum melting furnace. The ingots were further hot rolled to 15 mm in thickness, cooled to room temperature, heated to 900 °C in a laboratory atmosphere furnace, and then normalized by air cooling. The microstructures of the materials observed by optical microscopy are shown in  Fig. 1 
                         . As shown in  Fig. 1 , these steel samples showed ferrite/pearlite two-phase microstructures with different ferrite/pearlite fractions by carbon content. In addition, it should be noted that the grain size was different among these steel samples.

sections.heading: Prestrain test and Charpy impact test
paragraphs:
A prestrain test was carried out on the tested steel samples shown in  Fig. 1 . The prestrain condition is shown in  Table 2 
                         . In addition to the condition without prestrain, three prestrain conditions were prepared. P1 is a single prestrain condition, and P2 and P3 are cyclic prestrain conditions assuming a large earthquake. The prestrain test specimen and an example of a hysteresis loop that is generated during the tension and compression tests are shown in  Fig. 2 
                         . As shown in  Fig. 2 (a), the test specimen was machined from the mid-thickness position, and the prestrain direction was set to the rolling direction. The amount of prestrain shown in  Table 2  was plastic strain excluding the elastic part and was monitored experimentally by using strain gauges.

After the prestrain test, three standard V-notch Charpy impact test specimens were machined so that the crack opening direction was in the prestrain direction, as shown in  Fig. 2 (a). Charpy impact tests were carried out in accordance with ISO148 [ 32 ], under various temperatures, and 12 test specimens were tested for each prestrain condition. To compare the damage accumulation in each phase among the three materials, high magnification microstructure observations were carried out by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The samples for TEM observation were cut from “As” and after load pattern “P3”, mechanically thinned to a thickness of less than 0.1 mm, and punched into 3 mm discs in diameter. The conventional electropolishing method was performed using an electrolyte solution containing 5% perchloric acid and 95% acetic acid. The observation results are shown in  Fig. 4 
                         . For all the steel samples, there was no substantial change in the pearlite region before and after plastic prestrain, suggesting that plastic deformation is imposed mostly on the ferrite region. In the ferrite region, it is observed that the higher the ferrite fraction, the stronger the intragranular work-hardening structure that is formed is, especially in FP3, where the cell walls appear to be thick and strong due to intragranular dislocation tangles. In addition, the formation of dislocation cells in FP1, which has a small ferrite ratio, is moderate. The formation of dislocations in the ferrite portions seems to be the main cause of microcracks in the pearlite phase, which is consistent with the aforementioned trend of the change in the brittle fracture initiation characteristics by Charpy impact testing.

To quantitatively discuss the mechanisms for the relationships between brittle fracture toughness and microstructural factors, the mechanical aspects need to be further investigated. In the next section, the material damage accumulation rule for brittle fracture will be discussed by using several FEM analysis methods.

sections.heading: Material damage analysis by the continuum-mechanics-based FEM
paragraphs: In this section, the material damage estimation rule is discussed using FEM analysis based on conventional continuum mechanics (CMFEM). The prestrain tests described in the previous chapter were simulated, and the effective damage was calculated based on the concept of effective damage strain determined by the back stress updating method [ 23 , 24 ].

sections.heading: Simulation of the prestrain test
paragraphs:

Isotropic hardening expresses the magnitude of the yield surface, and kinematic hardening expresses the movement of the yield surface. sections.heading: Material damage analysis by the FEM incorporating the crystal plasticity model
paragraphs:
In this section, the material damage estimation rule was discussed using strain gradient plasticity (SGP), one of the computational models based on crystal plasticity theory. SGP is the theory suggested by Ashby et al. [ 36 ], and many studies on SGP formulations have been carried out by several researchers [ 37–40 ]. The conventional macroscopic model has discussed values averaged over the whole, rather than each crystal value even when the steel material is polycrystalline. To understand the phenomenon of polycrystallinity, it is important to simulate polycrystallinity, and calculations based on the plastic deformation of polycrystals can be carried out by using SGP theory. In addition, SGP theory is relatively easy to apply because SGP can perform highly accurate calculations with a relatively smaller calculation load than the strict Crystal Plasticity Finite Element Method (CPFEM). As mentioned in chapter 1, brittle fracture in steel is considered to occur mainly due to piled-up dislocations, so it is important to understand dislocation movement to comprehend the material damage mechanism. SGP can calculate two types of dislocation densities: geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) and statistically stored dislocations (SSDs). The GND depends on the gradient of plastic strain, and the SSD depends on the equivalent plastic strain. Martínez et al. The prestrain test was simulated by coding this theory in the Abaqus User Element (UEL) software, one of the Abaqus user subroutines [ 43 ]. 8-Node quadratic isoparametric element was used for grain interior element, and 6-Node interface node was used for grain boundary element. In this analysis, the simulation was carried out by the static implicit methods. As mentioned above, the steel used in this paper has a ferrite/pearlite two-phase microstructure, so the two-phase microstructure was simulated by changing the constitutive equation in this analysis. Pearlite fractions of these steel materials obtained from 2D observations of the microstructure are FP1: 60%, FP2: 35%, and FP3: 20%, but the area fraction is trimmed off a portion of the cross-sectional area. Here, the volume fraction is assumed to be equivalent to the area function obtained from the cross-sectional analysis [ 44–46 ]. In addition, not only the fraction of pearlite but also the grain diameter and thickness of pearlite were different among these steels.  Table 4 
                       shows the area fraction obtained from the 2D observation of the microstructures, the average grain diameter, and the thickness of pearlite. FEM models describing the microstructure tested were created based on the information shown in  Table 4 . Additionally, the increase in the yield stress by ferrite grain refinement based on the Hall-Petch equation [ 4 , 5 ] is included in the SGP calculation, so only the yield stress of sufficiently coarse ferrite grains needs to be determined from tensile tests. However, pearlite is a layered structure of cementite and ferrite, and its yield stress is controlled by the lamellar spacing [ 29 , 47 ]. It is difficult to precisely measure the lamellar spacing for each steel, so the yield stress was determined based on the assumption that the lamellar spacing is uniformly 0.2μm. In executing SGP, we used the Swift-type flow stress relationships shown in Eq.  (9) , and each material constant was determined as shown in  Table 5 
                      . Additionally, the microstructure models (not mesh division), where each material parameter is given in each area, are shown in  Fig. 6 
                      . The grain geometries in these models are determined as a combination of simple hexagons and ellipses to meet the parameter requirements shown in  Table 4 . In addition, there are about 300 elements in each ferrite grain.

Prestrain test simulations were carried out using the simplified microstructure models shown in  Fig. 6 . In the ferrite/pearlite two-phase microstructure, the ferrite grains are considered to mainly undergo plastic deformation and dislocations pile up adjacent to the pearlite structure. Then, piled-up dislocations are thought to repel each other and apply forces to the grain boundaries [ 4 , 5 ]. Thus, it is considered that all the dislocations in each ferrite grain have an effect on the adjacent pearlite structure. Based on this concept, the total dislocation density in each ferrite grain ( ρ 
                      α ) was a good index for describing the amount of material damage.  Fig. 7 
                       shows the history of  ρ 
                      α  for each model. As shown in  Fig. 7 ,  ρ 
                      α  basically increased while repeating small increases and decreases. This is because  ρ 
                      GND, α  temporally decreased when load reversal occurred, which led to a decrease in  ρ 
                      α . In fact, it has been experimentally confirmed that there are intervals where material damage does not progress for load reversal when cyclic prestrain is loaded [ 24 , 25 ].  Fig. 7  also shows that the damage histories and distribution of the plastic strain and dislocation density were substantially different among the models. One reason is thought to be due to the difference in pearlite proportion. The degree of concentration of plastic deformation in the ferrite grain varies as the pearlite proportion changes. In addition, not only the proportion of pearlite but also the grain diameter and thickness of pearlite were different. The damage evolution history strongly depends on the grain diameter because  ρ 
                      α  is the total dislocation density in each ferrite grain.

In this way, material damage can be estimated with high accuracy by simulating the microstructure with SGP. In the next chapter, based on these results, a parametric analysis will be carried out by modeling various microstructures, and the key to new damage-resistant materials will be examined.

sections.heading: Parametric analysis for examining damage-resistant materials
paragraphs: In this chapter, damage-resistant materials were examined by using SGP analysis based on the validity of the index verified in the previous chapter. From an engineering point of view, materials need to not only be resistant to damage but also have high strength. Generally, it is known that high strength and high toughness can be achieved by grain refinement, but refinement requires a very high level of technology and usually high cost. In this study, as a first trial, damage-resistant materials were examined by varying the ratio of soft and hard phase microstructures while keeping the grain size constant. In addition, the soft phase is always assumed to be the ferrite phase throughout the parametric analysis, and hard phase is assumed to be various phase, for example pearlite, martensite, and bainite.

First, the effect of soft and hard phase proportions was investigated. The grain diameters in both phases were fixed at 15μm, and the hard phase proportion varied from 20% to 60%. The material flow curves of the soft and hard phases were the same as those shown in  Table 5 , and the prestrain conditions were the same as those shown in  Table 2 . Next, the effect of the placement of the hard phase was investigated. The hard phase proportion was fixed at 60%, and the microstructures where the hard phase was isolated and interconnected were compared.  Fig. 9 (b) shows the change in  ρ

This is because plastic deformation not only concentrates on the soft phase but also occurs in the hard phase when the hard phase is interconnected, so the concentration on the plastic deformation in the soft phase is relaxed. This phenomenon agrees with past research [ 48 ].

Finally, the effect of the difference in the yield stress between the soft phase and hard phase was investigated. In the case where ferrite is regarded as a soft phase, the yield stress of the hard phase can be varied by changing the microstructure, for example, pearlite, bainite and martensite. Here, it is assumed that the yield stress of the soft phase was fixed at 120 MPa, and only the yield stress of the hard phase was changed. This difference may be interpreted by the fact that plastic deformation occurred even in the hard phase when the hard phase proportion was high, while plastic deformation hardly occurred in the hard phase when the fraction of the hard phase was small, and plastic strain occurred only in the soft phase, so the strength and material damage did not change very much. However, the strength increases because the hard phase undergoes plastic deformation when the fraction of the hard phase is large. In addition, the amount of plastic deformation in the soft phase is likely to increase as the difference between the yield stress of the soft and hard phases increases, which increases both the strength and material damage. In this context, as shown in  Fig. 10 (b), it was revealed that when the hard phase proportion is reasonably large and the hard phase is interconnected, a favorable balance in which the strength is sufficiently large and the amount of damage is small can be obtained.

In this section, the factors affecting the amount of damage and strength are discussed, and a principle of the microstructure of the material that can achieve both high strength and damage resistance is proposed by a parametric analysis using the microstructure model incorporating SGP. However, this model is only adaptable to dual phase material, and more detailed development of the material will be a subject for future work since a more comprehensive investigation of various factors, such as the manufacturability and welding properties, is required.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
In this paper, the effect of the microstructure on toughness deterioration due to prestrain was investigated by loading cyclic prestrains onto steel plates with different microstructures assuming that the structural steel materials were subjected to large earthquakes or unexpected large ocean waves. In addition, discussion with FEM analysis incorporating the SGP theory that was specially developed by the authors based on the experimental results was carried out. Using this novel FEM analysis method, the key principle of a damage-resistant material was finally suggested. The obtained findings are listed below: 
                         
                            1) 
                            It was experimentally confirmed that the Charpy impact toughness deteriorated due to cyclic prestrain in three kinds of ferrite/pearlite steels. The amount of toughness deterioration varies very much among different microstructures, which is not explained by the conventional material damage estimation rule, such as the Coffin-Manson equation. Additionally, the existence of steel material resistance to damage from prestrain was proven. 
                         
                         
                            2) 
                            It was revealed that material damage due to brittle fracture can be evaluated by using the effective damage strain with back stress updating proposed by Ohata et al. [ 23 ]. Material damage was appropriately estimated by simulating a prestrain test using a combined hardening rule. This approach is advantageous because it requires only conventional FEM analysis; however, the accuracy is not ideal, and this is not suitable for detailed microstructural studies. 
                         
                         
                            3) 
                            It was shown that material damage can be estimated by simulating the microstructure with high precision based on the SGP theory. Material damage can be evaluated based on the micromechanism of brittle fracture by calculating the dislocation density distribution. 
                         
                         
                            4) 
                            Damage-resistant materials with sufficient strength can be proposed by a parametric analysis with varying microstructures by using SGP theory. It was suggested that when the hard phase proportion is reasonably large and the hard phase is interconnected, the strength is sufficiently large and the amount of damage is small.

In this study, applying a new crystal plasticity model (SGP theory) to FEM analysis, many new findings about the effect of the microstructure on material damage due to prestrain, which has not been clarified so far, were presented. However, some steel materials also contain microstructures other than those in current research, not only ferrite/pearlite two-phase microstructures but also more complicated microstructures, such as bainite or martensite. Each microstructure has a different damage mechanism, and it is important to investigate these micromechanisms for brittle fracture initiation first. The effect of precipitates such as cementite or MA and complicated microstructures such as bainite or martensite on prestrain embrittlement should be investigated in the future.
